sections.h2: What should a Wyoming home seller know about the state first?
sections.html:
Wyoming is the smallest state by population and the tenth largest by area, so a house sale here depends heavily on which town and county the property sits in. The state has about 588,800 residents spread over roughly 97,800 square miles, and it is divided into 23 counties.

Cheyenne is the capital and the largest city at about 65,100 people. Casper follows at about 59,000, then Gillette at about 33,400, Laramie at about 31,400 and Rock Springs at about 23,500. Federal agencies manage nearly half of the land, which is one reason private lots in some counties are scarce and why a rural parcel can look very different from a city lot on paper.

The western half of the state is mostly Rocky Mountain ranges. The eastern half is high plains. The Continental Divide runs north to south through the middle, and the Great Divide Basin is a region where water cannot reach an ocean. A seller in Jackson and a seller in Lusk are working in two different housing worlds, even though both pay tax under the same state framework.

sections.h2: Which Wyoming counties are the largest, and where are their seats?
sections.html:
Laramie County is the most populous county in Wyoming and Niobrara County is the least. The table below lists the ten largest counties by the latest census count along with the smallest, so you can see where your county falls.

sections.h2: How does the Wyoming economy affect home sales?
sections.html:
Energy and minerals drive much of Wyoming's economy, and that shows up in local housing demand. Coal, natural gas, oil, uranium and trona are the major drivers, and the state holds the world's largest known trona reserve. Tourism around Yellowstone and Grand Teton National Parks adds billions of dollars in visitor spending each year, and livestock, hay, sugar beets, wheat and barley round out agriculture.

Wyoming has no individual or corporate income tax, which is part of why property and mineral taxes carry so much of the load for local governments. In 2025, mineral production made up about 44 percent of assessed valuation statewide, and residential property was about 30 percent.

For a seller, the practical point is that a house in a mineral county can be tied to the fortunes of one industry. Campbell County had the largest assessed valuation in 2025 at about $4.84 billion, while Sublette County's valuation fell about 55 percent that year. Those swings change local budgets and mill levies, and they are part of why a buyer's lender or an investor will ask about the local job base before making an offer.

sections.h2: What does Wyoming weather mean for the condition of a house?
sections.html:
Wyoming is drier, windier and subject to bigger temperature swings than most of the country. Much of the state gets under 10 inches of rain a year, while mountain areas can receive 20 inches or more, much of it as snow. The record high is 114 degrees and the record low is minus 66 degrees.

Those extremes are the reason inspectors and buyers look closely at a few things:

  • Roofing and flashing, because wind and freeze-thaw cycles wear them quickly.
  • Furnace age and insulation, since heating a house through a long cold season is a major cost.
  • Foundation cracks and drainage, especially where spring snowmelt collects near the walls.
  • Well and septic condition on rural lots outside municipal service.

A seller can repair before listing, accept a lower price, or sell as-is to a buyer who budgets for the work.

sections.h2: How does Wyoming property tax work for a seller?
sections.html:
Wyoming property tax is valued by the county assessor, set by local mill levies, and collected by the county treasurer. The Legislature sets the assessment ratio, which is 9.5 percent of market value for residential property. The tax equals market value times the ratio times the total mill levy divided by 1,000, and one mill is $1 per $1,000 of assessed value.

The statewide average mill levy in 2025 was 65.280 mills, but it varies by county. Teton County averaged 57.772, Natrona County averaged 72.238, and Big Horn County had the highest at 73.826. Two identical houses can carry different tax bills just because they sit in different taxing districts.

Property is valued as of January 1, and Laramie County notes that assessment schedules go out no later than the fourth Monday in April, with written objections due within 30 days of mailing. The county board of equalization issues decisions by October 1.

sections.h2: When is Wyoming property tax due, and what happens if it is late?
sections.html:
Wyoming property tax is paid in two halves: the first is payable by November 10 and the second by May 10 of the following year. State law lists the first half as due on or after September 1 and payable on or after November 10, and the second half as due on or after March 1 and payable on or after May 10.

Paying the full amount by December 31 avoids interest on the first half. A balance that is not paid by its payable date becomes delinquent and accrues 18 percent interest per year. The Laramie County treasurer also notes that taxes remain owed even if the bill never arrives, and that mortgage escrow accounts may pay on your behalf.

ItemWhat the sources say
First half payableBy November 10

Tax sale noticePublished once a week for three weeks

Real property taxes are a perpetual lien on the property, so unpaid tax follows the house to a new owner. Ask the county treasurer for a payoff figure before closing.

sections.h2: What tax relief programs exist for Wyoming homeowners?
sections.html:
Wyoming offers several relief programs, and a seller should know which ones the house is already using. The largest is the 25 percent residential exemption passed in 2025, which covers 25 percent of the first $1 million of a home's value for owner-occupied houses, condominiums, townhouses and manufactured homes.

  • The exemption requires full-time residency of at least eight months of the year, with limited military exceptions, and an affidavit filed with the county assessor. For the latest year the filing deadline was March 1.
  • The property tax refund program, which received $10.5 million in 2025, helps households whose income is at or below 145 percent of the county median.
  • The veteran exemption rose from $3,000 to $6,000 in 2024.
  • Residents aged 65 or older who have paid Wyoming property taxes for at least 25 years can receive a 50 percent reduction.

Because the exemption depends on owner occupancy, a house that becomes a rental or a vacation home after a sale may be treated differently for the buyer. Ask the assessor how a change of use affects the next bill.

sections.h2: What are the transfer and recording steps when a Wyoming house sells?
sections.html:
A Wyoming deed is recorded with the county clerk, and it must be accompanied by a sworn statement from the buyer or the buyer's agent. Under W.S. 34-1-142, that statement discloses the names of the parties, the sale date, a legal description, the price and the payment terms, along with an estimate of any personal property included.

The statement is not a public record. County and state officials must keep it confidential, and it can be disclosed only to someone reviewing or contesting a property tax assessment. Certain transfers, such as gifts of more than half the property's value, nominal transfers between spouses or parents and children, and tax or foreclosure sales, may omit the price and terms.

Deeds must also be acknowledged before a notarial officer. A related rule in W.S. 34-1-112 says a conveyance is not void just because someone else is in actual possession of the land and claiming it adversely. In plain terms, you can still sell a house that someone is occupying without permission, although the buyer inherits the problem unless you resolve it first.

sections.h2: How do probate and foreclosure affect a Wyoming sale?
sections.html:
Wyoming has shortcuts for small estates and a power-of-sale foreclosure process, and both can change how quickly a house can be sold. A 2025 law raised the small estate limit from $200,000 to $400,000, effective July 1, 2025, for the affidavit and summary distribution procedures. The waiting periods did not change: 30 days after death for heirs and 90 days for government creditors.

Foreclosure in Wyoming usually runs by advertisement. In the 2010 text of the statutes we reviewed, the lender mails written notice at least ten days before publication begins, and the sale notice then runs for four consecutive weeks in a county newspaper. The sale is held at the courthouse, and a sale that skips the statute's requirements is void. That version also describes a three-month redemption period after the sale, with a twelve-month period for qualifying agricultural land. Statutes change, so confirm the current text with a Wyoming attorney.

faqs.q: How many counties does Wyoming have?
faqs.a: Wyoming has 23 counties. Laramie County is the most populous and Niobrara County is the least populous.

faqs.q: When are Wyoming property taxes due?
faqs.a: The first half is payable by November 10 and the second half by May 10 of the following year. Unpaid balances become delinquent after those dates and accrue 18 percent interest per year.

faqs.q: Does Wyoming have a state income tax?
faqs.a: No. Wyoming has no individual or corporate income tax, which is why property and mineral taxes are important to local budgets.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Wyoming house that has back taxes?
faqs.a: Yes, but the taxes are a perpetual lien on the real property, so they are normally paid from the sale proceeds at closing. Ask the county treasurer for a payoff figure before you sign anything.

faqs.q: What is the small estate limit in Wyoming?
faqs.a: The limit is $400,000 for the affidavit and summary distribution procedures, effective July 1, 2025. Heirs can use the affidavit 30 days after death.
